text: Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs. HNSW organizes vectors into a layered proximity graph. The top layers are sparse and hold long-range links; each layer below is denser and more local. A search starts at the single entry point in the highest layer, descends greedily, and performs a best-first expansion at the base layer. Query cost is roughly logarithmic in the number of vectors rather than linear. The parameter efSearch trades recall against latency at query time, which means an operator can tune it without rebuilding the index. The construction parameter efConstruction controls graph quality. Error code ANN-4417 is emitted when the entry point is missing.

Inverted file indexes with product quantization. An IVF index partitions the vector space with k-means and searches only the nprobe nearest partitions. Combined with product quantization, which splits each vector into subvectors and replaces each with a codebook centroid, memory drops by an order of magnitude at some cost in accuracy. IVF-PQ suits billion-scale corpora where the raw vectors do not fit in memory. Recall is governed by nprobe. Unlike a graph index, IVF supports efficient deletion.

metadata.title: Inverted file indexes with product quantization

text: Okapi BM25 term weighting. BM25 scores a document by summing, over query terms, an inverse document frequency weight multiplied by a saturating term-frequency factor. The parameter k1 controls how quickly repeated occurrences stop adding value, and b controls how strongly document length is normalized. Because BM25 matches surface forms, it excels at rare identifiers, product codes and proper nouns, and fails whenever the query and the document express the same idea in different words.

Dense passage retrieval with bi-encoders. A bi-encoder embeds queries and passages independently into a shared vector space, so passage vectors are computed once offline and a query needs only one forward pass plus a nearest-neighbour lookup. Because matching happens in embedding space, a bi-encoder retrieves passages that paraphrase the query without sharing any words. The weakness is the mirror image of BM25's: a rare literal token has little training signal and its embedding carries little information.

Hybrid retrieval and rank fusion. Hybrid retrieval runs a lexical and a dense retriever and merges their rankings. Reciprocal rank fusion combines by rank position, assigning each result a weight of one over a constant plus its rank, which avoids comparing incommensurable score scales. Weighted fusion normalizes scores first and preserves the margin between a strong and a weak match. Hybrid retrieval helps most when the two retrievers disagree; when they return the same documents there is nothing to gain.

Chunking strategies for retrieval. Chunk size is a trade-off. Large chunks dilute the embedding with unrelated content so nothing matches strongly; small chunks lose the surrounding context that makes a passage answerable. Overlap between adjacent chunks prevents the sentence answering a question from being cut in half at a boundary. Recursive splitting on paragraph and sentence boundaries preserves semantic units better than fixed character windows.

Cross-encoder reranking. A cross-encoder reads the query and a candidate passage together in a single forward pass, so attention can relate query tokens directly to passage tokens. It is substantially more accurate than a bi-encoder and far too slow to score a whole corpus, so it is used as a second stage over the top fifty or hundred candidates from a cheap first-stage retriever. This cascade is the standard architecture in production search.

Retrieval evaluation metrics. Recall at k asks whether the relevant document was retrieved at all and bounds everything downstream. Precision at k asks how much of the retrieved set was useful. Mean reciprocal rank rewards placing the first correct result near the top. Normalized discounted cumulative gain uses graded relevance and discounts by log of rank, so it distinguishes a relevant result at position one from the same result at position nine.

Grounding and hallucination in RAG. A retrieval-augmented system hallucinates when it answers from parametric memory instead of the retrieved context. Two mitigations matter in practice: instructing the model to say it does not know when the context is insufficient, and requiring inline citations that map to specific retrieved passages. Verbatim span checking catches wholesale invention but not a plausible paraphrase of something never retrieved.

Embedding models and asymmetry. Many retrieval embedding models are asymmetric: queries and passages are encoded with different instructions or prefixes, because a short question and a long passage have very different surface statistics. Using the passage encoding for a query measurably degrades retrieval. Normalizing vectors to unit length makes the dot product equal to cosine similarity, which lets a single matrix multiply serve as the scoring function.

Vector quantization and memory. Scalar quantization stores each dimension in eight bits instead of thirty-two, cutting memory by four with little recall loss. Binary quantization goes further, storing one bit per dimension and using Hamming distance, then rescoring the top candidates with full-precision vectors. The rescoring step is what makes aggressive quantization viable.

Tail latency in search systems. Average latency hides the user experience. A system with a five millisecond median and a four hundred millisecond ninety-ninth percentile feels very different from one that is uniformly twelve milliseconds. Percentiles should be measured with nearest-rank so a reported number corresponds to a request that actually happened. In a fan-out architecture the slowest shard determines the response time.
